title: Campaigns & Lawyers React as Trump DOJ Seeks to Block Election Results If Sullivan Loses】
body:
A federal lawsuit filed by former President Donald Trump’s legal team seeks to block the certification of Alaska’s 2024 Senate election results if incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan fails to retain his seat, prompting a flurry of denials and accusations from both the campaign and the state’s Democratic leadership. The suit, which alleges that the election was “fraudulently administered” and that Sullivan’s office engaged in “illegal coordination” with the Trump administration, has been dismissed by legal experts as a politically motivated attempt to keep the incumbent in power and to sow doubt in the electoral process.

Trump’s attorneys, led by former White House counsel John L. Miller, argue that the Department of Justice (DOJ) should intervene to halt the certification of the vote, citing alleged irregularities in absentee ballot handling and claims that Sullivan’s campaign benefited from “unlawful federal assistance.” The filing, submitted to the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska on October 24, asserts that the DOJ has a statutory duty to protect the integrity of federal elections and that failure to act would constitute a “gross miscarriage of justice.” The court, however, has yet to schedule a hearing, and legal scholars warn that the case faces steep hurdles, including standing, jurisdiction, and the lack of concrete evidence.

Sen. Sullivan’s campaign quickly rebuffed the allegations, labeling them “categorically false” and emphasizing that the senator has repeatedly denied any involvement with the Trump administration’s post‑election maneuvers. “We have no knowledge of any wrongdoing, and we will vigorously defend the legitimacy of this election,” said a spokesperson for the campaign. The statement also noted that the lawsuit appears designed to distract from the substantive issues facing Alaskans, such as rising energy costs and infrastructure needs, and to capitalize on the heightened partisan tensions surrounding the 2024 midterms.

Alaska’s Democratic Representative to the Senate, Representative Mary Peltola, echoed the campaign’s dismissal and framed the lawsuit as a “political machination” by the incumbent to cling to power. Peltola’s office released a detailed response, pointing out that the DOJ has already concluded its investigations into the 2022 and 2024 election cycles with no findings of fraud or misconduct. “The Trump administration’s attempt to weaponize the Justice Department against a duly elected official undermines the very foundations of our democratic system,” the statement read. Peltola added that the lawsuit threatens to erode public confidence in Alaska’s electoral process, which historically enjoys high voter participation and trust.

Legal analysts suggest that the suit is unlikely to succeed on procedural grounds. Professor Alan R. Kelley of the University of Washington’s School of Law noted that the DOJ’s role is advisory rather than interventionist in state elections, and that any claim of “illegal coordination” would require substantial proof that has not been presented. Moreover, the courts have consistently rejected attempts by candidates to preemptively block election certification, citing the principle that disputes should be resolved after votes are cast and counted. “This filing is more about political theater than legal merit,” Kelley said.

The controversy arrives at a pivotal moment for Alaska’s political landscape. The Senate race, traditionally a stronghold for Republicans, has become increasingly competitive, with Democratic challenger Sarah Miller gaining traction on issues such as climate policy and indigenous rights. If Sullivan were to lose, the lawsuit could set a precedent for future candidates to challenge election outcomes through the federal courts, potentially destabilizing the orderly transfer of power. Observers warn that even an unsuccessful suit could have lasting repercussions, fueling mistrust among voters and encouraging similar tactics in other swing states.

Looking ahead, the court’s response to the filing will be closely watched by both parties. Should the judge dismiss the case, it may reinforce the judiciary’s reluctance to intervene in state election certifications and curb the spread of litigation aimed at overturning results. Conversely, a more favorable ruling for Trump’s team could embolden further legal challenges, prompting Congress and the DOJ to clarify the limits of federal involvement in state elections. As the final weeks of the campaign unfold, the focus is likely to shift back to policy debates and voter outreach, with the lawsuit serving as a cautionary reminder of how legal strategies are increasingly intertwined with political maneuvering.
